title: Barchester Towers
description: Published in 1857, the most celebrated of the Barsetshire novels and the fullest comedy of ecclesiastical politics in English: the struggle for the bishopric and the wardenship at Barchester between the High Church party of the archdeacon and the new Low Church bishop and his wife.
plot_or_argument: Bishop Proudie dies and is succeeded by Dr Proudie, whose wife and chaplain Mr Slope dominate him; Slope schemes to become warden of Hiram's Hospital and to marry Eleanor Harding, and is defeated in both by the arrival of the Stanhope family and by the comic catastrophe of the bishop's tea party. Mr Arabin becomes the new warden, and Eleanor marries him.
principal_characters: Mrs Proudie; Bishop Proudie; Mr Slope; Archdeacon Grantly; Mr Arabin; Eleanor Harding; Obadiah Slope; Bertie Stanhope; Charlotte Stanhope; Dr Stanhope; Signora Neroni; Mr Quiverful; Miss Thorne
historical_context: The 1850s and the party divisions of the Church of England, the clergy's families and their finances, and the arrival of the Low Church Evangelical party into the cathedral close.
literary_significance: Barchester Towers is the classic English novel of ecclesiastical intrigue and one of the funniest novels of the nineteenth century; its narrator's constant commentary and its slow rotation of sympathy set the manner for the whole of Trollope's later work and for the Victorian novel of institutional life.

title: Doctor Thorne
description: Published in 1858: the Barsetshire novel most openly about money, in which the illegitimate niece of a country doctor turns out to be the heiress of the railway fortune of the Scatcherd family.
plot_or_argument: Dr Thorne's niece Mary, the daughter of his dissolute brother and of a Scatcherd, is loved by Frank Gresham, the heir of a ruined squire; Frank's family demands a wealthy marriage, and the novel follows their opposition until Mary's inheritance is established and the estate is saved by her fortune.
principal_characters: Dr Thorne; Mary Thorne; Frank Gresham; Squire Gresham; Lady Arabella Gresham; Beatrice Gresham; Roger Scatcherd; Louis Scatcherd; Augusta Gresham; Mr Moffat
historical_context: The railway contractors and the new industrial wealth of the 1840s-50s, the landowning gentry's debt, and the marriage market as the mechanism by which estates were preserved.
literary_significance: Doctor Thorne is Trollope's most direct study of the marriage market and of the relation between landed and industrial wealth, and the novel is the best single guide to the economics of Victorian courtship. Its treatment of illegitimacy is unusually free of moralising for its date.

title: Framley Parsonage
description: Serialised in the first number of the Cornhill Magazine (January 1860) and published in three volumes: the novel that made Trollope famous and established the Cornhill as the leading magazine of the 1860s.
plot_or_argument: Mark Robarts, the young vicar of Framley, is drawn into the debts of the fashionable MP Nathaniel Sowerby and is ruined by an accommodation bill; he is saved by Lord Lufton's intervention and by his sister Lucy's marriage to the heir, and the novel's subplots follow the patronage politics of the Barsetshire living and the social season in London.
principal_characters: Mark Robarts; Fanny Robarts; Lucy Robarts; Lord Lufton; Lady Lufton; Nathaniel Sowerby; the Duke of Omnium; Griselda Grantly; Lord Dumbello; Mr Crawley
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (The Cornhill Magazine, 1860); three volumes 1861
historical_context: The 1850s-60s, the magazine boom of the Cornhill, the culture of the country-house visit and the London season, and the political parties of the Palmerston era.
literary_significance: Framley Parsonage is the point at which the serial novel and the new monthly magazine became the central literary institution of the 1860s, and it shows Trollope's mature management of a large cast across three interlocking plots. Its accurate notation of a young clergyman's debts is one of the best-documented pictures of the economics of genteel life in the period.

title: The Small House at Allington
description: Serialised in the Cornhill in 1862-64 and published in 1864: the Barsetshire novel of the broken engagement, and the book in which Trollope's heroine Lily Dale refuses to marry after being jilted.
plot_or_argument: Lily Dale is engaged to Adolphus Crosbie, who breaks the engagement to marry the daughter of a countess; she refuses the faithful love of Johnny Eames, who has loved her since childhood. The subplot follows the courtship of Crosbie's own unhappy marriage and the ambitions of the de Courcy family.
principal_characters: Lily Dale; Johnny Eames; Adolphus Crosbie; Alexandrina de Courcy; Lady Julia de Courcy; the Earl de Courcy; Mrs Dale; Bell Dale; Bernard Dale; Christopher Dale
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (Cornhill); two volumes 1864
historical_context: The 1860s, the season and the marriage market, the position of the unmarried woman, and the world of the minor aristocracy and its hangers-on.
literary_significance: The Small House at Allington is Trollope's deepest study of disappointed love and the most argued-about ending in his work: Lily Dale's refusal to marry has been read both as a failure of the marriage plot and as one of the earliest English novelistic defences of a woman's right to choose singleness.

title: The Last Chronicle of Barset
description: Published in twenty-four monthly parts from December 1866 to July 1867, and the close of the Barsetshire series: the trial of the Rev. Josiah Crawley for the theft of a cheque, and the deaths of Bishop and Mrs Proudie.
plot_or_argument: Mr Crawley, the impoverished perpetual curate of Hogglestock, is accused of stealing a cheque and is suspended from his duties; the novel follows his pride, his daughter Grace's engagement to Major Grantly, and the at last revealed source of the cheque. Mrs Proudie dies of a heart attack, the bishop marries again, and the series closes with the dispersal of the Barsetshire characters.
principal_characters: Josiah Crawley; Grace Crawley; Major Henry Grantly; Archdeacon Grantly; Mrs Proudie; Bishop Proudie; Lily Dale; Johnny Eames; Mr Toogood; Lady Lufton
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (24 numbers); two volumes 1867
historical_context: The ecclesiastical courts of the 1860s, the poverty of the assistant clergy, and the world of the cathedral close at the end of its ascendancy.
literary_significance: The Last Chronicle is the most ambitious of the Barsetshire novels and one of the first English novels to submit its central character to a trial at law: its portrait of Crawley's intellectual pride and spiritual torment is the finest thing Trollope wrote, and its killing-off of Mrs Proudie is one of the most famous authorial decisions in Victorian fiction.

title: Phineas Finn, the Irish Member
description: Published in twenty monthly parts in 1867-69: the first of the political novels of the Palliser series, and the first full English novel of the working of Parliament seen from the back benches.
plot_or_argument: Phineas Finn, an Irish barrister's son without money or connections, enters Parliament for an Irish borough and rises through two ministries; he is tried for the murder of a political rival and acquitted, and the novel follows his courtship of three women — the rich and sensible Madame Goesler, the aristocratic Laura Standish, and the Irish Mary Flood Jones.
principal_characters: Phineas Finn; Madame Max Goesler; Laura Standish; Mr Kennedy; Violet Effingham; Lord Chiltern; Mary Flood Jones; Mr Monk; Lord Cantrip; the Duke of Omnium; Barrington Erle; Mr Daubeny
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (20 numbers); two volumes 1869 (Palliser, 2)
historical_context: The Reform Bill of 1867 and the parliamentary session of the 1860s, the Irish question, the party whips and the lobby, and the expense of standing for Parliament.
literary_significance: Phineas Finn is the founding novel of parliamentary life in English and the best account in fiction of how a Victorian political career was actually made. Its Irish hero makes it a central text for the study of the Union, and the figure of Madame Goesler is among Trollope's finest portraits of the independent woman.

title: The Eustace Diamonds
description: Serialised in the Fortnightly Review (1871-72) and published in 1873: Trollope's nearest approach to the sensation novel, the story of a beautiful and unscrupulous widow and a diamond necklace that may or may not be an heirloom.
plot_or_argument: Lizzie Greystock, the widow of Sir Florian Eustace, claims the family diamonds as her own property against the trustees of the estate; a burglary, a trial and the collapse of her engagement to Lord Fawn follow, and the novel's second plot follows the political career of Phineas Finn and the fortunes of Lucy Morris.
principal_characters: Lizzie Eustace; Lord Fawn; Frank Greystock; Lucy Morris; Phineas Finn; Mr Camperdown; Sir Florian Eustace; Lady Glencora Palliser; the Duke of Omnium
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts; three volumes 1873 (Palliser, 3)
historical_context: The Married Women's Property Act of 1870 and the law of heirlooms, the sensation vogue of the 1860s-70s, and the parliamentary politics of the Gladstone ministry.
literary_significance: The Eustace Diamonds is the most deliberate of Trollope's experiments in the sensation mode, and its heroine is one of the great comic-structural villains of Victorian fiction. The novel is also an exact legal and social study of the position of a married woman's property in the years of the first Married Women's Property Act.

title: The Way We Live Now
description: Published in twenty monthly parts from February 1874 to September 1875, and the most savage of Trollope's novels: a study of the financial swindler Augustus Melmotte and of the society that is willing to be swindled by him.
plot_or_argument: Melmotte, a financier of unknown origin, launches the Great South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway in London and is received into the highest society; his daughter Marie's fortune draws suitors, and the collapse of the railway and Melmotte's forgery and suicide destroy the world that had courted him. The novel's second plot follows the ruined squire Roger Carbury and the love of Paul Montague for Hetta Carbury.
principal_characters: Augustus Melmotte; Marie Melmotte; Sir Felix Carbury; Roger Carbury; Hetta Carbury; Paul Montague; Lady Carbury; Hamilton K. Fisker; Mr Broune; Mr Booker; Lord Nidderdale; Dolly Longestaffe
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (20 numbers); two volumes 1875
historical_context: The railway speculation of the early 1870s, the failure of the Overend and Gurney bank in 1866 and the memory of the Crédit Mobilier, the London season, and the political corruption of the period.
literary_significance: The Way We Live Now is the great Victorian novel of financial capitalism and of the corruption of the press and politics by money; Trollope's own estimate that it was his best book has been widely accepted since the twentieth century, and its portrait of a society that knows it is being swindled and does not care has kept it the most modern of his novels.

title: The Prime Minister
description: Published in 1875-76: the central political novel of the Palliser series, in which Plantagenet Palliser becomes Prime Minister in a coalition and his wife's social campaign makes him impossible.
plot_or_argument: The Duke of Omnium forms a coalition government and becomes Prime Minister without the support of either party; Lady Glencora's entertainment of the adventurer Ferdinand Lopez, her political meddling and the accusation that her husband has used his office for private advantage destroy the ministry. The subplot follows Lopez's fraudulent speculations, his marriage to Emily Wharton, and his suicide.
principal_characters: Plantagenet Palliser; Lady Glencora Palliser; Ferdinand Lopez; Emily Wharton; Mr Wharton; Everett Wharton; Lady Eustace; Sextus Parker; Mr Gresham; Sir Orlando Drought
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts; four volumes 1876 (Palliser, 5)
historical_context: The coalition ministries of the 1850s-70s, the political hostess and the dinner party as instruments of government, and the financial fraud of the mid-1870s.
literary_significance: The Prime Minister is the most sophisticated English novel about the routines of political power, and its portrait of the Duke's constitutional conscience is unmatched in fiction. Lady Glencora Palliser is one of the great creations of Victorian fiction, and the Lopez plot is a masterly study of the confidence trick as a social form.

title: The Duke's Children
description: Published in 1879-80, the last of the Palliser novels: the widowed Duke's struggle with his three children, each of whom wishes to marry against his wishes.
plot_or_argument: The Duke of Omnium, now out of office and mourning Glencora, finds that his son and heir Lord Silverbridge wants to marry the American Isabel Boncassen, that his daughter Mary loves the impoverished Frank Tregear, and that the younger son Gerald has been sent down from Cambridge. The novel resolves in the Duke's recognition that his children's choices are worthy of respect.
principal_characters: Plantagenet Palliser; Lord Silverbridge; Lady Mary Palliser; Gerald Palliser; Isabel Boncassen; Frank Tregear; Lady Mabel Grex; Mr Boncassen; Major Tifto
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts; three volumes 1880 (Palliser, 6)
historical_context: The late 1870s and the first appearance of the American heiress in English society, the decline of the landed estate, and the rise of the professional politician.
literary_significance: The Duke's Children is the most personal and the most formally elegant of Trollope's political novels, and its study of a father's pride is one of the finest things in Victorian fiction. It closes the Palliser series on a note of reconciliation that the twentieth century found unexpectedly moving, and it is a key text for the study of transatlantic marriage.

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
description: Published in 1884 and the founding novel of American vernacular prose: the story of Huck Finn and the runaway slave Jim on a raft down the Mississippi, told in Huck's own voice.
plot_or_argument: Huck escapes his drunken father, joins Jim on Jackson's Island, and the two drift down the river through a series of encounters with feuding families, confidence men, lynch mobs and a revival meeting; Huck's decision to help Jim escape, taken against everything his society has taught him, is the moral centre of the book, and the ending at the Phelps farm brings Tom Sawyer's romantic schemes and Jim's freedom.
narrative_structure: First-person vernacular narrative in forty-three chapters, with a series of episodic river adventures.
principal_characters: Huckleberry Finn; Jim; Tom Sawyer; Pap Finn; the Duke; the Dauphin; Aunt Sally Phelps; the Grangerfords; the Shepherdsons; the Widow Douglas
historical_context: The 1830s-40s: the slaveholding South before the Civil War, the Mississippi river towns, and the American debate on race and Reconstruction at the time of composition.
literary_significance: Huckleberry Finn is the central American novel and the founding text of American vernacular prose: its first-person voice, its ironies about race and its river journey made it the source of modern American fiction, and its treatment of slavery and freedom is the most debated subject in American literary criticism.

title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
description: Published in 1876 and the most popular boys' book in American literature: the childhood of Tom Sawyer in the Mississippi river town of St Petersburg, and the buried treasure of Injun Joe.
plot_or_argument: Tom plays hooky, whitewashes a fence, attends his own funeral, runs away to Jackson's Island, falls in love with Becky Thatcher, and with Huck witnesses the murder of Dr Robinson in the graveyard; the novel ends with the treasure found and Huck taken into the Widow Douglas's house.
principal_characters: Tom Sawyer; Huckleberry Finn; Becky Thatcher; Aunt Polly; Injun Joe; Muff Potter; Sid Sawyer; Mary; the Widow Douglas
historical_context: The 1840s: the Mississippi river town of Hannibal, the American Sunday school and the temperance movement.
literary_significance: Tom Sawyer is the classic American book of boyhood and the fount of the American literature of childhood: it created the image of the river town and made Hannibal a national place, and its portrait of a boy's freedom is one of the permanent American idylls.

title: Life on the Mississippi
description: Published in 1883 and the finest American book about a river and a trade: a memoir of Twain's apprenticeship as a riverboat pilot, followed by a return voyage down the Mississippi in 1882.
plot_or_argument: The first half recounts the author's training as a pilot under Horace Bixby, the lore of the river and the science of reading its currents; the second half describes the post-war river, the decayed towns, the new railroads and the changes of a quarter-century.
historical_context: The 1857-82: the steamboat era, the Civil War and its closing of the river, and the American railway age.
literary_significance: Life on the Mississippi is a classic of American autobiography and the central book about the American river: its account of piloting is one of the great pieces of technical writing in English, and its record of the river's decline is a permanent document of American economic history.

title: Roughing It
description: Published in 1872 and the great American book of the western frontier: Twain's account of his years as a silver prospector and newspaperman in Nevada and California.
plot_or_argument: Twain travels by stagecoach to Nevada, tries mining and fails, becomes a reporter in Virginia City, hears the tall tales of the frontier, visits the Sandwich Islands, and returns to the East with the material that made him a writer.
historical_context: The 1861-66: the Nevada silver rush and the Comstock Lode, the overland stage, and the new journalism of the western mining camps.
literary_significance: Roughing It is the central American book of the frontier and the finest comic travel narrative in American literature: it records the myth of the West at the moment of its making and it is the source of the cowboy and the mining camp in American popular culture.

title: The Prince and the Pauper
description: Published in 1881 and Twain's first attempt at historical fiction: the story of two identical boys, one a prince and one a pauper, who exchange places in Tudor England.
plot_or_argument: Tom Canty, a London beggar, and Prince Edward exchange clothes and are taken for one another; the prince is driven out into the streets and experiences the cruelty of his own laws, while Tom rules in his place until the coronation scene restores the true king.
historical_context: The 1547: the reign of Edward VI, the English vagrancy laws, and the American democratic critique of monarchy.
literary_significance: The Prince and the Pauper is the most popular American historical novel of the century for children and a key text in the American literature of democratic equality; its picture of Tudor England shaped the American image of the English past.

title: Pudd'nhead Wilson
description: Published in 1894 and the darkest of Twain's novels: the story of a slave woman who switches her son with her master's heir, and of the lawyer who solves the case by fingerprints.
plot_or_argument: Roxy, a slave who is one-sixteenth black, exchanges her son Chambers with the master's son Tom; the false Tom grows up as a vicious white gentleman and the true heir as a slave, and the lawyer Wilson, the 'pudd'nhead' of the town, proves the exchange by fingerprints at the trial for murder.
principal_characters: Roxy; Tom Driscoll; Valet de Chambre (Chambers); David Wilson; Judge Driscoll; Percy Driscoll; Patsy Cooper
historical_context: The 1830-50s, the slave society of a Missouri river town, the new science of fingerprinting, and the American debate onrace and heredity.
literary_significance: Pudd'nhead Wilson is the central American novel of racial passing and one of the first detective novels in American literature: its use of fingerprints and its treatment of slavery as a system of identity-theft make it a key text for the study of race in America.

title: The Rise of Silas Lapham
description: Published in 1885 and the central American novel of business: the story of a self-made paint manufacturer who loses his fortune, and of the moral choice that makes his ruin a rise.
plot_or_argument: Silas Lapham, a Vermont farmer's son turned paint magnate, moves to Boston and tries to marry his daughter into the Brahmin class; his speculation in stocks fails, he refuses a fraudulent offer to save himself at the expense of others, and the family returns to Vermont, where Lapham finds his true dignity.
principal_characters: Silas Lapham; Persis Lapham; Irene Lapham; Penelope Lapham; Tom Corey; Bromfield Corey; Anna Corey; Bartley Hubbard; Milton K. Rogers
historical_context: The 1870s-80s: the American paint and mineral trade, the Boston Brahmins, and the Gilded Age business cycle.
literary_significance: The Rise of Silas Lapham is the finest American novel of business and the central text of American realism: its portrait of the self-made man and its argument that moral failure can be worldly success made it the model for the American business novel.

title: A Hazard of New Fortunes
description: Published in 1890 and Howells's masterpiece: a panorama of New York in the Gilded Age, built around the founding of a literary magazine and the streetcar strike of 1889.
plot_or_argument: Basil March moves from Boston to New York to edit a new magazine financed by the rich and capricious Dryfoos; the magazine's staff, the Dryfoos family, and the socialist Lindau and the artist Beaton are drawn into the strike, a riot and a death, and the novel ends with the failure of the enterprise and the dispersal of its people.
historical_context: The 1889-90: the New York streetcar strike, the Haymarket aftermath, the new mass magazines, and the socialist movement in America.
literary_significance: A Hazard of New Fortunes is the central American novel of the Gilded Age city and the finest American social novel of the nineteenth century: its panoramic method and its treatment of class, labour and immigration made it the model for the American urban novel from Dreiser to Dos Passos.

title: A Modern Instance
description: Published in 1882 and the first American novel to treat divorce as a serious subject: the marriage and separation of Marcia Gaylord and Bartley Hubbard.
plot_or_argument: Bartley Hubbard, a charming and unscrupulous journalist, marries Marcia Gaylord and moves from Maine to Boston; his gambling and infidelity destroy the marriage, Marcia takes their child and leaves him, and the novel ends with Bartley's death in a western mining town and Marcia's return to her family.
principal_characters: Bartley Hubbard; Marcia Gaylord; Squire Gaylord; Ben Halleck; Clara Kingsbury; Olive Halleck; Kinney
historical_context: The 1870s-80s: the American divorce law, the new journalism, and the Boston of the 1870s.
literary_significance: A Modern Instance is the founding American novel of divorce and a key text in the American literature of marriage: its portrait of an unhappy marriage and its treatment of the legal and social consequences made it a landmark of American realism.

title: Indian Summer
description: Published in 1886 and the wittiest of Howells's comedies of manners: a middle-aged American bachelor in Florence is tempted by a beautiful young woman and consoled by a woman of his own age.
plot_or_argument: Theodore Colville, a Chicago journalist burnt out at forty, returns to Florence where he had loved as a young man; he becomes engaged to the dazzling young Imogene Graham, discovers the impossibility of the match, and marries the widowed Mrs Bowen, whose good sense and irony have been the novel's chorus.
principal_characters: Theodore Colville; Imogene Graham; Lina Bowen; Mrs Graham; Morton; Effie Bowen
historical_context: The 1885-86: the American colony in Florence, the international theme of the American abroad, and the Howellsian comedy of ordinary life.
literary_significance: Indian Summer is the finest of Howells's light comedies and one of the best American novels of the 1880s: its portrait of a man growing old among the monuments of Europe is a masterpiece of American irony, and it shows Howells at his most Jamesian in the international setting.

title: Criticism and Fiction
description: Published in 1891 and the manifesto of American realism: the essays from the 'Editor's Study' in which Howells argued for the truthful treatment of ordinary American life.
plot_or_argument: Howells attacks the romantic and the sensational in fiction, praises the realism of Jane Austen, George Eliot, Tolstoy and Turgenev, and argues that the American novel must concern itself with the smiling aspects of the common life rather than with the exceptional and the violent.
historical_context: The 1886-91: the American debate on realism, the international copyright question, and the rise of the mass magazine.
literary_significance: Criticism and Fiction is the founding statement of American literary realism and one of the most influential books of American criticism: it set the terms of the debate between romance and realism that dominated American fiction until the 1920s.

title: The Bostonians
description: Published in 1886 and the great American novel of the women's movement: the struggle between a southern conservative and a Boston feminist for the soul of a young orator.
plot_or_argument: Verena Tarrant, a gifted speaker, is taken up by the Boston reformer Olive Chancellor and groomed for the women's cause; Olive's cousin Basil Ransom, a Mississippi lawyer, falls in love with Verena and persuades her to abandon the platform for marriage, and the novel ends with her escape from the hall on the night of her great speech.
principal_characters: Olive Chancellor; Verena Tarrant; Basil Ransom; Mrs Luna; Selah Tarrant; Miss Birdseye; Dr Prance
historical_context: The 1870s: the Boston women's movement, the American suffrage campaign, and the post-war South.
literary_significance: The Bostonians is the central American novel of the women's movement and one of the most complex treatments of same-sex attachment in nineteenth-century fiction: its portrait of Olive Chancellor and its analysis of the politics of reform made it a key text of American feminist criticism.

title: The Portrait of a Lady
description: Published in 1881 and James's first masterpiece: the story of Isabel Archer, an American heiress in Europe, and of the marriage that imprisons her.
plot_or_argument: Isabel Archer comes to England with her aunt, refuses two good offers of marriage, and is persuaded by Madame Merle to marry the aesthete Gilbert Osmond; the discovery that Osmond and Madame Merle have used her for her money is the crisis of the novel, and she returns to Rome at the end, bound by a promise and by her own sense of honour.
principal_characters: Isabel Archer; Gilbert Osmond; Madame Merle; Ralph Touchett; Lord Warburton; Caspar Goodwood; Pansy Osmond; Henrietta Stackpole; Daniel Touchett; Countess Gemini
historical_context: The 1870s: the American heiress in Europe, the international marriage market, and the position of married women under English law.
literary_significance: The Portrait of a Lady is the central American novel of the international theme and one of the great novels of the nineteenth century: its study of a woman's freedom and its anatomy of a bad marriage made it the model for the modern novel of consciousness, and Isabel Archer is the most fully realised American heroine in fiction.

title: The Ambassadors
description: Published in 1903 and generally regarded as James's finest novel: the story of Lambert Strether, sent to Paris to bring back a young American, and of the education that changes his mission.
plot_or_argument: Strether is sent by Mrs Newsome to Paris to rescue her son Chad from a presumably disreputable life; he discovers that Chad's attachment to the Countess de Vionnet is a relationship of real value, and he returns to America alone, having 'not, out of the whole affair, got anything for myself'.
principal_characters: Lambert Strether; Chad Newsome; Madame de Vionnet; Maria Gostrey; Waymarsh; Mrs Newsome; Sarah Pocock; Jim Pocock; Little Bilham
historical_context: The 1900s: the American expatriate in Paris, the international marriage market, and the Puritan inheritance in American culture.
literary_significance: The Ambassadors is the most perfectly constructed novel in English and the central text of James's late manner: its 'central consciousness' method and its treatment of the American failure to live made it the model for the modern psychological novel, and it is the book in which James's theory of fiction is fully realised.

title: The Wings of the Dove
description: Published in 1902 and the most morally complex of James's late novels: the story of a dying American heiress and the couple who plan to inherit her fortune.
plot_or_argument: Kate Croy and Merton Densher, too poor to marry, scheme to secure the fortune of Milly Theale, a dying American heiress; Densher wins Milly's love, refuses the money after her death, and is left with the knowledge that he has lost both women and the moral ground he thought he had kept.
principal_characters: Milly Theale; Kate Croy; Merton Densher; Maud Lowder; Susan Shepherd Stringham; Lord Mark; Sir Luke Strett
historical_context: The 1900s: the London and Venetian society of the international set, and the American fortune in Europe.
literary_significance: The Wings of the Dove is the finest of James's late novels and the central text of the modern novel of moral ambiguity: its treatment of money, illness and the corruption of love made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of consciousness, and Milly Theale is one of the most memorable heroines in American fiction.
